title: Rush
author: Castelino, Jo
summary: Jo Castelino opens with a minute-by-minute narrative of a rushed, low-level-chaotic 50-minute lesson, a Do Now that starts too slowly, cold-calling that reveals more students knew an answer than were asked, mini-whiteboard routines that need constant policing, a booklet task compressed into the last ten minutes, to argue that many "good practice" techniques fail not because they're wrong but because there simply isn't enough time to execute them well. Her diagnosis is that low-level disruption and disorganisation eat the time that should go to retrieval, quizzing, and explanation, producing a rush that leaves students able to "parrot back simple facts" without deep understanding. Her proposed fix is standardising and routinising the mechanical parts of a lesson so they stop consuming conscious attention: a detailed table walks through specific student expectations, where equipment goes, how students enter, how the Do Now is formatted, what happens when a student is stuck, how homework is set, alongside exactly how she implements and enforces each one and why it saves time. She is explicit that efficiency is not the same as making lessons "soulless": the point of routinising the mechanics is to free up time for the deeper thinking and connection-making that routines alone can't produce.
points: Castelino's core distinction is between lessons that look busy (retrieval Do Nows, MWB checks, praise) and lessons that are actually efficient; the former can still leave "not enough time" for retrieval, quizzing, reviewing, and explaining to happen properly.

Her "hands must be down during review, up during questioning" rule ties directly to Cold Call: reviewing a Do Now or independent practice task assumes students have already had thinking time, so no additional wait time is warranted there.

Her mini-whiteboard protocol, hide while writing, face down when done, hold up on signal, keep up unrubbed until instructed, is designed specifically to prevent students copying answers and to give the teacher time to review most boards before moving on.
She frames standardised, low-drama routines as the precondition for spending saved time on deeper understanding, not as an end in themselves.
quotes: There is low level chatter, low level confusion, a low level of being disorganised. There is not enough time for retrieval, not enough time for quizzing, not enough time for reviewing, not enough time for explanations.

This is not to say that lessons should be efficient but soulless periods of time where students and teachers behave like robots. But being efficient means there can be time to explore concepts in greater depth, ensure students can truly transfer their understanding and make strong connections between schemas.

By hiding the board and placing it face-down, other students will find it harder to get their answers from their partner’s board. By leaving the boards unrubbed, I have time to review most (if not all) of them and then have the option to provide feedback that can be immediately implemented by students on their boards.
A review always follows a part of the lesson where students have had time to think already and so I can use Cold Call with more confidence than if students have not had any time to think.
Doing these things does not magically give me loads of time but it does make focusing on deeping understanding easier.
